similar effects to primary reinforcement for

some learners. Fiske et al. found that the effects

tems were variable for one of two learners;
whereas, the current study found that the

results for Annie and Jack were consistent

across two component sequences. The current

lower than those observed under EXT. This

token was novel (as in Fiske et al.) or was asso-

ciated with a history of pairing with primary

reinforcement. Collectively, the results of these
two studies highlight the importance of using

high-quality backup reinforcement in token

systems.

decisions.reason: Under Codebook Step 2, a target must be a study whose published empirical finding is re-tested rather than a work supplying the assay/task or background comparisons. Fiske et al. (2019) adopt the multiple-schedule reinforcer assessment (MSA) procedure from Smaby et al. (2007; 10.1002/bin.242, shipped and base-blind target 0) and the star-pointing task and fixed sequence from Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013; 10.1002/jaba.67, base-blind target 1). Although the Discussion notes MSA viability/suitability and full bodies of Smaby (2007), Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013), and Fiske et al. (2015) remain unavailable (without inferring invisible findings), the current study does not manipulate social-consequence forms or prompt-dependency differential reinforcement (tokens-plus-praise vs. either alone). Likewise, the verified complete Leon, Borrero, and DeLeon (2016; 10.1002/jaba.311) primary manuscript tests parametric post-response time delays (0-120 s) under FR-1 food/token/exchange schedules, whereas Fiske et al. (2019) compare response-based FR-5/10 yoked schedules only as a post-hoc mechanistic contrast. By contrast, Fiske et al. (2019) explicitly design their MSA evaluation to re-test Fiske et al. (2015; 10.1002/jaba.207, verified via abstract and reference list, 'Assessing the value of token reinforcement for individuals with autism')—replacing lengthy progressive-ratio schedules and directly corroborating Fiske et al.'s (2015) empirical findings on token-versus-primary reinforcement efficacy and low unpaired/no-backup token responding.

raw_new_expert_decision.reason: Although the authors state that they sought to 'systematically replicate Smaby et al. (2007) and Cividini-Motta and Ahearn’s (2013) use of the MSA', the full text establishes that Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013; 10.1002/jaba.67, 'Effects of two variations of differential reinforcement on prompt dependency') supplied the assessment procedure, star-pointing task (Method, p. 3, lines 477-489), and fixed component order (Design, p. 4, lines 655-663) rather than a retested empirical finding. Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013) tested differential reinforcement variations (tokens plus praise vs. either alone) to reduce prompt dependency, whereas Fiske et al. (2019) evaluate token-economy components (token without backup, yoked FR, token with backup, primary reinforcement) and compare those substantive findings to Fiske et al. (2015) in the Discussion (pp. 5-6, lines 886-926). Under the codebook, reusing an assessment method, task, or design from an earlier study without retesting its empirical finding is not an omitted replication target.
